findings.reason: This logs the full AWS secret key value, which is a secret credential and should not appear in logs.
findings.fix: Remove the value from the log or replace it with a non-reversible placeholder/redaction.

findings.reason: This logs the AWS session token in cleartext, leaking a live credential.
findings.fix: Delete this log line or log only a non-sensitive marker such as token length or a fixed redaction string.

findings.reason: This base64-encodes and logs the full serialized delegation-token container, which can expose embedded credentials.
findings.fix: Do not log the payload bytes; keep only a success/failure message or a non-sensitive byte count if needed.

findings.reason: The REST client SSL context explicitly disables endpoint identification, so hostname verification is turned off for REST TLS connections.
findings.fix: Set the endpoint identification algorithm to the default HTTPS verification mode instead of null, or only disable it behind an explicit, narrowly-scoped compatibility option.

verificationSteps: Run the relevant unit tests for S3 delegation-token acquisition/receipt and confirm logs no longer contain secret key, session token, or serialized token payload values.
Add/adjust a test that captures logging for AbstractS3DelegationTokenProvider.init() and AbstractS3DelegationTokenReceiver.onNewTokensObtained() and asserts secrets are redacted.
Add a REST TLS client test that inspects the created SSL context/engine configuration and verifies hostname verification is enabled for REST endpoints.
Manually inspect generated log output from a token refresh cycle to confirm only redacted markers or non-sensitive metadata remain.
uncertainties: I did not see the surrounding call sites, so I cannot confirm whether the logging paths are reachable in all deployments, only that the source logs secrets when executed.
The SSL hostname-verification issue is clearly present in the REST client context builder, but I cannot verify from these snippets whether any higher-level code compensates for it elsewhere.

findings.reason: REST client TLS hostname verification is explicitly disabled here, so the client will not verify the peer hostname against the server certificate.
findings.fix: Remove the null override and let endpoint identification remain enabled for REST clients, or set the appropriate HTTPS hostname verification algorithm only when a vetted exception is required.

findings.reason: This logs the raw AWS secret access key value, which is sensitive credential material.
findings.fix: Do not log the secret key value; remove the message or replace it with a non-sensitive constant such as a presence/length indicator.

findings.reason: This logs the keystore password in cleartext at info level, exposing a secret used to load private-key material.
findings.fix: Remove this log line or replace it with a redacted placeholder; never emit the password itself.

findings.reason: This logs the AWS session token value, which is a live credential secret.
findings.fix: Delete the log statement or log only a constant/status message without the token value.

verificationSteps: Search the four files for any remaining logs that interpolate secret material (passwords, secret keys, session tokens) and confirm only redacted/status-only logging remains.
Run a unit test or targeted static check that exercises S3 delegation token init/receive paths and assert log output never contains the configured secret key, keystore password, or session token.
Create a REST client SSL context from SSLUtils and confirm the resulting Netty SSL context no longer disables endpoint identification; verify the peer hostname is checked during TLS handshake.
Re-run existing REST-over-TLS connection tests against a certificate whose SAN/CN does not match the host and confirm the client now fails hostname verification.
uncertainties: I did not inspect call sites or deployment settings, so I cannot determine whether the REST TLS hostname check is additionally overridden elsewhere.
